items.name: mattpocock/skills
items.author: Matt Pocock
items.take: A curated collection of composable engineering skills for AI coding agents — TDD, architecture improvement, code review, bug diagnosis, domain modeling, and requirements grilling — installable via the skills CLI into any compatible agent.
items.why: It hit ~3,360 stars in a single day because it turns ad-hoc agent prompting into disciplined, reusable workflows that embed engineering best practices directly into how agents operate.
items.explanation: Each skill is a prompt + process pack with explicit When to Use, Prerequisites, Workflow, and Verification sections, so agents follow the same decision path a senior engineer would rather than guessing. The collection covers the full development lifecycle and installs with one command (npx skills add mattpocock/skills) into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other agentskills.io-compatible tools. The project is MIT-licensed and explicitly designed as a community standard rather than a vendor lock-in.

items.name: MoneyPrinterTurbo
items.author: Harry0703
items.take: An end-to-end automated pipeline that turns a topic or keyword into HD short-form videos (9:16 or 16:9) — AI script, material sourcing, TTS, subtitles, BGM, and render — with WebUI, CLI, API, and auto-post to TikTok/IG/YouTube Shorts.
items.why: It's at ~114k total stars and gained ~1,200 in one day because it compresses the entire short-form video production workflow into a single runnable command, making high-volume content creation practical for solo creators.
items.explanation: The pipeline chains multiple models: an LLM for scriptwriting, stock footage or AI generation for visuals, TTS for narration, and FFmpeg for assembly. It supports multi-language, aspect-ratio switching, and batch generation. Quality depends on your API keys and model choices; the project is open-source (MIT) but running it well requires decent GPU resources or cloud credits. For teams doing regular short-form content, it replaces a multi-tool manual workflow with a reproducible, version-controlled process.

items.name: career-ops
items.author: Santifer
items.take: A local-first AI job search command center that scans portals, scores listings A–F, tailors ATS-optimized CVs and cover letters per role, tracks applications, and researches companies — all running inside your existing AI CLI (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) with no cloud dependency.
items.why: It gained ~920 stars in a day at ~67.5k total because it solves a real, painful workflow: job hunting is high-volume, repetitive, and privacy-sensitive, and existing tools either spam applications or require uploading your career data to a SaaS.
items.explanation: The tool installs as an agent skill and uses your local LLM to parse job descriptions, match against your experience, generate tailored documents, and maintain a local application tracker. Scoring uses a transparent rubric (role fit, compensation signal, company health, etc.) rather than a black-box model. It's MIT-licensed and runs entirely locally, so credentials and personal data never leave your machine. The main caveat is that portal scraping selectors can break when sites redesign, so expect periodic maintenance.

items.name: Zetta
items.author: air-embodied-brain (Tsinghua AIR)
items.take: Zetta is a closed-loop embodied harness that evolves code-based runtime critics and recovery skills online while keeping the base policy frozen, achieving 90.8% on LIBERO-Pro and 93.6% on RoboCasa with an 11.1x inference speedup.
items.why: It represents a fundamental shift in embodied AI — instead of training massive end-to-end policies, it keeps the base model frozen and learns self-correcting critics and recovery skills at runtime, delivering SOTA results with dramatically less compute.
items.explanation: Zetta operates on three timescale-separated loops: action-frequency critics that govern execution in real time, rollout-level critic/recovery proposals, and validation-gated skill updates that distill verified failures into reusable skills. The accompanying Z-Infra rollout layer decouples agent logic from heterogeneous hardware (CPUs, GPUs, simulators), scaling valid rollout throughput 20.6x on 8×A100 GPUs. Learned skills transfer zero-shot across tasks, and clear robotic "Aha Moments" emerge where the agent discovers novel recovery behaviors. The paper (arXiv:2608.16590) and code are fully open; the AGPL-3.0 license is worth noting for commercial embedding.

items.name: SPADE
items.author: spade-rl (UW, Stanford, CMU, MIT, NUS, SNU, UChicago)
items.take: SPADE (Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments) makes environment design itself a learnable component: a designer agent generates progressively harder interactive environments as executable Python while a solver agent improves on held-out math, science, code, and reasoning benchmarks past the saturation point of fixed-environment baselines.
items.why: It introduces a genuinely new self-improvement loop where the environment adapts to the agent's growing capabilities, breaking the plateau that plagues fixed-curriculum approaches — the paper shows consistent gains on Qwen3 models at 4B, 8B, and 30B-A3B scales across cognitive games and multi-turn tool use.
items.explanation: A single shared policy plays both roles via role-specific prompts. The Environment Designer samples grounding context from a 15k-document math/science corpus and an accumulated environment memory, then writes complete executable environments with Gym-style reset()/step() interfaces and privileged hints. The Reasoning Agent plays each environment with and without the hint; the gap in return (hint-based regret) trains the designer to target environments at the agent's capability frontier. Training uses GRPO with Slime/SGLang (SGLang inference, Megatron-LM updates, Ray orchestration) and a Tinker backend. Checkpoints, the static GPT-5.5 environment corpus (7,872 validated environments), and all training recipes are released on Hugging Face. MIT-licensed.

items.name: Autolith
items.author: luciusmagn
items.take: Autolith is a programming agent with a live Common Lisp runtime that can directly inspect, modify, and evolve its own code image — using SBCL's introspection and the Lisp image paradigm for true self-modifying agent loops rather than file-based tool calls.
items.why: It's a radically different agent architecture: the agent lives inside a running Lisp image, giving it native access to all symbols, REPL-driven development, and the ability to checkpoint/restore entire cognitive states — something file-based agents fundamentally cannot do.
items.explanation: Autolith runs entirely inside an SBCL image on Linux x86-64 (macOS arm64 via Nix), with a pinned binary release that includes its own SBCL, Lisp dependencies, and a bubblewrap sandbox helper. It talks directly to Codex and Grok subscription APIs (no CLI wrapper). The agent owns its model loop, tools, conversations, authentication, live mutation with private commits, checkpoints, and a pristine recovery image it can reload into if things go wrong. Nix is the recommended install path (nix run github:luciusmagn/autolith). MIT-licensed. The tradeoff: model-generated Lisp runs with your user privileges, so it's a development agent, not a security sandbox.
